title: Nature and art types of reunion: Nyssen's quicksilver; potter, glass, chemistry — Cap. 9 close
pass_a_gloss: Hitherto we have seen that the resurrection belonging toward the flesh stands as possible. if a lye prepared from the ashes of nettles stands as exposed to cold, in that ice the nettles offer themselves to be seen. The fourth finally stands as of chemical art: for from sand and nitre transparent glass stands as made, and there stand as also glasses from ashes. The third stands as belonging toward the glassmaker's art: The second stands as the golden Achilles who formerly had been bronze. so also God our bodies. For just as the potter forms a vessel from clay and dries it in the sun, but if by chance it stands as broken and reduced to clay he reshapes and restores it: The first stands as belonging toward the potter's art, which Gregory of Nyssa uses in his third oration On the Resurrection. But the types of art stand as various. and he declares that by the example of quicksilver. touching which Gregory of Nyssa, who wrote three most learned orations on Christ's resurrection, in the book which the ancients called On Structure, On the Making of Man chapters 25, 26, and 27, teaches that the soul by affection and love from a singular nature pursues the body in whose quasi-companionship it stood as, and by an ineffable pull of nature stands as carried to its conjunction; But to the thing:
pass_b_english: But to the thing: concerning which Gregory of Nyssa, who wrote three most learned orations on Christ's resurrection, in the book which the ancients called On Structure, On the Making of Man chapters 25, 26, and 27, teaches that the soul by affection and love from a singular nature pursues the body in whose quasi-companionship it was, and by an ineffable pull of nature is carried to its conjunction; and he declares that by the example of quicksilver.

But the types of art are various. The first is of the potter's art, which Gregory of Nyssa uses in his third oration On the Resurrection. For just as the potter forms a vessel from clay and dries it in the sun, but if by chance it is broken and reduced to clay he reshapes and restores it: so also God our bodies. The second is the golden Achilles who formerly had been bronze. The third is of the glassmaker's art: for from sand and nitre transparent glass is made, and there are also glasses from ashes. The fourth finally is of chemical art: if a lye prepared from the ashes of nettles is exposed to cold, in that ice the nettles offer themselves to be seen. Hitherto we have seen that the resurrection of the flesh is possible.
source_text: Ad rem vero, de quo Gregorius Nyssenus, qui de resurrectione Christi tres doctissimas scripsit orationes, libro quem Structurae veteres dixerunt, de structura hominis cap. 25. 26. & 27. docet, animam affectione & amore a natura singulari corpus, in cujus quasi contubernio fuit, prosequi, & ineffabili naturae tractu ad ejus conjunctionem ferri; idque hoc exemplo declarat vivum argentum. Artis vero typi sunt varii. Primus est figulinae artis, quo utitur Gregorius Nyssenus orat. 3. de resurrectione. Sicut enim figulus vas e luto fingit & ad solem exsiccat, forte autem confractum & redactum in lutum refingit restituitque: ita & Deus corpora nostra. Secundus est Achilles aureus qui prius fuerat aeneus. Tertius est artis vitriariae: nam ex arena & nitro perspicuum vitrum efficitur, sunt etiam vitra e cineribus. Quartus denique est artis chymicae: e cineribus urticarum paratum lixivium si frigori exponatur, in glacie illa urticae conspiciendae sese praebent. Hactenus vidimus resurrectionem carnis esse possibilem.
